summary:
Poland does not criminalise consensual same-sex conduct; the 1932 Penal Code decriminalised it with an equal age of consent of 15, reaffirmed in 1948, and homosexuality was removed from the disease list in 1991. The current legal framework nonetheless leaves trans visitors exposed in several documented ways.

Legal gender recognition exists but is procedurally demanding. A trans person must obtain a medical diagnosis and undergo hormone replacement therapy before legal gender change; since the 1960s such changes have been performed. Because sterilising surgery is prohibited under Penal Code art. 156 §1 (with narrow medical exceptions), a trans person must change legal gender before sex reassignment surgery can proceed. Until March 2025 the process required litigation against one's own parents; on 4 March 2025 the Supreme Court's Civil Chamber resolved that recognition should proceed as a non-trial vital-records rectification on request, with the spouse as the only possible other participant and immediate effect upon a positive review. A 2015 Sejm-approved recognition bill allowing change without physical intervention was vetoed by President Duda in October 2015.

Detention and custody present documented health risks. On 13 March 2024 the Association for Legal Intervention reported that a regional court had placed a transgender Vietnamese woman in a guarded centre for male foreigners; after NGO intervention the Border Guard commander ordered her release, but her hormone therapy had been interrupted for three months because the centre refused to supply medication. Separately, on 11 July 2024 the European Court of Human Rights found that Polish prison authorities violated Article 8 of the Convention by denying a trans prisoner hormone replacement therapy and awarded EUR 8,000 in damages, establishing that medication denial in custody is litigable.

Hate-crime and hate-speech law does not currently cover gender identity. Poland's existing hate-crime provisions punish bias-motivated violence, threats, insults and promotion of hateful ideologies only where the victim's national, ethnic, racial, political or religious affiliation is the motive. Parliament passed an amendment on 6 March 2025 adding sexual orientation and sex or gender with up to three years' imprisonment for insulting or inciting hatred; President Duda declined to sign it on 17 April 2025 and referred it for constitutional review on free-expression grounds. A related Penal Code amendment adopted in March 2025 was referred to the Constitutional Tribunal and ruled unconstitutional on 30 September 2025, so the extended protections never entered into force.

Facilities and employment: in February 2025 the Supreme Court ruled that a non-binary casino dealer in Wrocław dismissed in 2021 for refusing female appearance rules requiring make-up, skirts and high heels had suffered gender-based discrimination, the first explicit Polish recognition that non-binary persons can face gender discrimination. Openly transgender people are officially barred from military service on medical grounds, with a gender dysphoria diagnosis resulting in automatic classification as permanently and completely unfit for service in both conflict and peace.

Relationship recognition remains unsettled. Article 18 of the Constitution places marriage as a union of a man and a woman under protection, and the Supreme Court, Constitutional Tribunal and Supreme Administrative Court have held this limits marriage to opposite-sex couples. On 20 March 2026 the Supreme Administrative Court ruled registries must recognise and transcribe marriage certificates of same-sex couples married in another EU member state, first implemented in Warsaw on 14 May 2026; on 28 July 2026 the Constitutional Tribunal ruled such transcription incompatible with the Constitution. On 29 May 2026 the Sejm passed the Act on the Status of the Closest Person granting limited notarised cohabitation rights, pending Senate and presidential approval that President Karol Nawrocki has opposed. In September 2024 the ECtHR ruled Poland's lack of partnership recognition leaves couples in an illegal vacuum violating their rights.

Public climate: after 2015 several municipalities and four voivodeships declared 'LGBT-free zones'. Administrative courts including the Supreme Administrative Court in June 2022 held such resolutions exceeded council powers and violated residents' dignity and private life; on 6 February 2024 the Warsaw Voivodeship Administrative Court annulled the last explicit anti-LGBT resolution (Mordy commune, 2019), while 11 similar discriminatory acts, including 10 Ordo Iuris Family Rights Charters, remained in force. On 20 July 2019 the first Equality March in Białystok with about 800 marchers was confronted by more than 4,000 counter-protesters throwing stones, bricks, firecrackers and bottles, requiring riot police intervention. On 7 August 2020 47 people were arrested in the Rainbow Night mass arrest, some peacefully protesting an activist's arrest. President Duda stated in the 2020 election that 'LGBT is not people, it's an ideology'.

Entry and harassment: Global Affairs Canada's travel advisory for Poland lists sexual orientation among reported harassment motives alongside physical appearance and foreigner status, and notes visa-free entry for tourists staying up to 90 days.
tangentialFactors:
Amnesty International's 2025 report 'A Thousand Cuts' documents technology-facilitated gender-based violence against Poland's LGBTI community on X, alongside the LGBT-free-zone legacy of 2019–23 and X's policy reversals (misgendering and deadnaming rule removed April 2023, reinstated 2024). This is an online abuse climate rather than a visitor-law exposure, but it shapes the public environment a visibly LGBTI or trans traveller enters.

ILGA-Europe's Annual Review 2025 records that a Deputy Justice Minister announced a hate-speech law extending protection to gender identity and sexual orientation, a March draft Penal Code amendment raised penalties for anti-LGBTI hate speech and violence and passed the Government Legislation Centre in May before approval was postponed, a second bill followed in late October, and the Prosecutor General set up a special response team with new guidelines for law enforcement. HRW's World Report 2025 describes LGBT-rights reform under the Tusk government as 'slow and insufficient', noting that in June 2024 Justice Minister Bodnar revoked the Ziobro directive that had blocked recognition of same-sex marriage certificates obtained abroad.

The 2019 EU LGBTI Survey II found 1 in 5 trans and intersex people in Poland were physically or sexually attacked in the past five years; this figure is a survey of trans and intersex respondents covering a window that closed in 2019 and is not a current prevalence measure.

Historical precedent for state-led censorship includes a 2007 proposal to punish anyone promoting homosexuality in schools with dismissal, fines or prison, ban LGBT organisations and safer-sex education, and fire teachers who reveal homosexuality. Operation Hyacinth of 15 November 1985 registered around 11,000 suspected gay men in a national database, and 'pink files' were still held by the Institute of National Remembrance as of 2005.
localsOnly:
Polish citizens changing legal gender must follow the Civil Status Records Law, Population Register Act and Identity Cards Act administrative regime, which a 2024 Przegląd Sejmowy analysis examines for equal treatment and adequacy of protection, particularly around civil status. Since 4 March 2025 the process is a non-trial vital-records rectification on request rather than litigation against one's parents.

Workplace and services: anti-discrimination provisions added to the Labour Code in 2003 ban employment discrimination on sexual orientation, and the equal-treatment law in force from 1 January 2011 prohibits sexual orientation discrimination in employment only. In 2019 the Constitutional Tribunal struck down the Petty Offence Code provision that had allowed the Supreme Court in 2018 to find a Łódź printer acted illegally in refusing banners for an LGBT group. The February 2025 Supreme Court ruling on the non-binary Wrocław casino dealer is the first explicit recognition that non-binary persons can face gender discrimination.

Resident-facing exposure: Poland's hate-crime law does not cover gender identity as a motivating characteristic, and the 2025 expansion was ruled unconstitutional on 30 September 2025. Openly transgender people are barred from military service on medical grounds. Same-sex couples cannot adopt and lesbian couples lack IVF access; limited rights include shared tenancy, refusal to testify as the closest person under Penal Code Article 115(11), and EU-law residency. The Sejm's 29 May 2026 Act on the Status of the Closest Person would add notarised cohabitation rights but awaits Senate and presidential approval that President Nawrocki opposes.

Support infrastructure includes the Trans-Fuzja foundation co-founded by MP Anna Grodzka, Campaign Against Homophobia (2001), and Lambda, registered by the Warsaw Voivodeship Court on 23 February 1990. Lambda's Queer Museum in Warsaw opened 6 December 2024 as the first of its kind in Central and Eastern Europe. The first recorded transgender meeting took place on 10 December 1985 at Warsaw's Department of Sexology, and the first sex reassignment surgery in Poland was performed in 1963 at Szpital Kolejowy in Międzylesie.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the 2026 Act on the Status of the Closest Person has completed Senate and presidential stages is unresolved in this record; the last documented position is Sejm passage on 29 May 2026 with presidential opposition noted.

The current practical availability of hormone replacement therapy in Polish prisons and guarded detention facilities after the July 2024 ECtHR judgment is not sourced here; the record documents the violation and damages but not subsequent compliance.

No current trans-specific violence rate with a denominator and period is available in this inventory; the 2019 EU LGBTI Survey II figure (1 in 5 trans and intersex people attacked in the prior five years) is a historical survey window and is not carried as a present prevalence measure.

Whether the 11 remaining discriminatory local acts documented as of February 2024 have since been repealed is unresolved in this record.
